title: Functions
summary: Name a piece of work once, then run it whenever you need it.
refresher: A **function** is a named block of code you can run whenever you want. You define it with `def`, **list** the **values** it needs in the parentheses, and call it by writing its name with parentheses after it. To hand a value back to the caller, use `return`. Printing is not returning: `print` shows text on the screen, while `return` gives a value your code can store and use. A function with no `return` hands back `None`.
refresher_code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

result = double(5)
print(result)
# 10

sections.title: What a function is
sections.summary: Define a reusable block of work and call it by name.

blocks.body: A **function** is a name for a piece of work. You describe the work once, then run it as many times as you like by writing its name. If you find yourself copying the same three lines into four places, that is a function asking to be written.

blocks.title: Follow a function call
blocks.caption: See arguments enter a function, a local variable appear, and return send the answer back.

steps.title: Call with arguments
steps.body: The caller sends 3 and 5 into the function.

steps.title: Parameters receive values
steps.body: Inside the function, a is 3 and b is 5.

steps.title: Return
steps.body: Return sends 8 back to the caller, and the function call is finished.

blocks.caption: Two steps that are easy to blur together. The `def` block only describes the work. Nothing happens until the last line runs it.
blocks.code:
def greet():
    print("Hello there!")

greet()
greet()

sections.title: Parameters and arguments
sections.summary: Pass **values** into a **function** and see how each call gets its own data.

blocks.body: Most **functions** need something to work with. You list the names for those values inside the parentheses of the `def` line. Those names are the **parameters**. The actual values you hand over when you call the function are the **arguments**. Same slot, two names, depending on which side you are standing on.

blocks.caption: Here `name` is the **parameter**, and the strings "Ada" and "Grace" are the **arguments**. The parameter is a variable that only exists while the **function** is running, and it holds whatever you passed in this time.
blocks.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello, " + name + "!")

greet("Ada")
greet("Grace")

sections.title: Trace one call at a time
sections.summary: A **function** call gets fresh parameter values, runs, then returns.

blocks.body: When a function confuses you, write one call on paper. Fill each parameter with the argument value, run the body in order, and replace the call with the returned value.

blocks.caption: Each call starts fresh. The parameter `name` holds Ada during the first call and Grace during the second.
blocks.code:
def label(name):
    word = "Hi " + name
    return word

first = label("Ada")
second = label("Grace")
print(first)
print(second)

blocks.prompt: What should you do first when tracing `subtract(10, 4)`?
blocks.code:
def subtract(a, b):
    return a - b
choices: Set a to 10 and b to 4
Run the return before filling parameters
blocks.why: Arguments fill parameters by position before the function body runs.

sections.title: Return vs print
sections.summary: Separate showing a **value** from giving the program a reusable result.

blocks.body: So far these **functions** only **print**. That is fine when the point is to show something to a person. It falls apart the moment your program needs the answer for itself. For that you need `return`.

blocks.caption: `return` hands a **value** back to whoever called the **function**. That value can be stored, added to, or passed along, which is the whole reason it exists. The result is 106.0 and not 106, because multiplying by 1.06 gives a decimal number.
blocks.code:
def add_tax(price):
    return price * 1.06

total = add_tax(100)
print(total)
print(add_tax(50) + add_tax(50))

blocks.title: print shows a value. return gives a value back.
blocks.body: If you take one thing from this lesson, take this one. `print` sends text to the screen for a human to read. Your program cannot pick that text back up and use it. `return` hands the **value** to the line that called the **function**, so it can be saved in a **variable** and used later. If you swap them, the screen may look exactly right while the program quietly has nothing to work with.

blocks.caption: Both **functions** look correct when you run them, because both put 8 on the screen. Only one of them lets the next line of code do anything with that 8.
blocks.wrong:
def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

result = add(3, 5)
print(result)
# 8
# None
blocks.right:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 5)
print(result)
# 8

blocks.body: The left version is not broken in an obvious way, and that is what makes it dangerous. A **function** with no `return` still hands something back. It hands back `None`, Python's way of saying "nothing here". So `result` becomes `None`, and any arithmetic you try on it later fails with a TypeError.

blocks.code:
def square(n):
    print(n * n)

answer = square(4)
print(answer)
blocks.why: The call to `square(4)` runs the **function**, and the `print` inside it puts 16 on the screen. But `square` has no `return`, so it hands back `None`. That is what lands in `answer`, and the last line prints it. If you picked "16 then 16", you assumed the printed **value** was also the returned value. It is not. Change `print(n * n)` to `return n * n` and you get 16 twice.

blocks.title: return also stops the function
blocks.body: The moment a `return` runs, the **function** ends. Any lines below it in the function body never run. That is useful when you want to exit early, and confusing when you did not mean to, so keep an eye on what you put after a `return`.

sections.title: Defaults, scope, and return paths
sections.summary: Use default **arguments**, understand local names, and make every path **return** when needed.

blocks.body: A **parameter** can have a default **value**. You give it one with an equals sign on the `def` line. If the caller leaves that **argument** out, Python uses the default. If they pass one, theirs wins.

blocks.caption: One **function**, two ways to call it. Defaults let you keep the common case short without giving up the option to be specific.
blocks.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return greeting + ", " + name + "!"

print(greet("Ada"))
print(greet("Ada", "Welcome"))

blocks.caption: **Variables** made inside a **function** live only inside it. That area is the function's scope. This program prints HEY, then crashes on the last line. Nothing was misspelled: `message` was born inside `shout` and was gone the moment `shout` finished, so `print(message)` asks for a name that no longer exists. Python stops the program and reports a NameError, showing a traceback that ends with the line `NameError: name 'message' is not defined`.
blocks.code:
def shout(word):
    message = word.upper()
    return message

print(shout("hey"))
print(message)

blocks.body: When Python hits an error it cannot handle, it stops and prints a traceback: several lines that name the **file**, the line that failed, and the error itself. The last line is the one that usually tells you what went wrong. Read tracebacks from the bottom up.

blocks.prompt: This **function** is supposed to **return** the larger of two numbers. What is wrong with it?
choices: It prints None, because no return runs when b is larger
It is a syntax error, since `if` needs an `else`
It prints 3, because the first parameter always wins
blocks.why: `a` is 3 and `b` is 9, so `a > b` is false and the indented `return a` never runs. The **function** reaches the end of its body with nothing returned, and a function that returns nothing hands back `None`. Python is fine with an `if` that has no `else`, so this is not a **syntax error**. It runs happily and gives you the wrong answer, which is the harder kind of bug to spot. Adding `return b` below the `if` fixes it.

blocks.title: A checklist for your next function
items: Give it a verb-shaped name that says what it does: `calculate_gpa`, not `stuff`.
Ask what it needs to know. Those become the **parameters**.
Ask what it should hand back. If the answer is anything at all, you need a `return`.
If a **value** ever gets stored or reused, **return** it. **Print** it only when a human needs to read it.
Check that every path through the **function** reaches a `return`, including the paths inside an `if`.
Test it by calling it and printing the result, not by trusting what the **function** prints on its own.

call-01.title: Definition is not execution
call-01.body: A function or method body waits until code calls it.
call-01.notice: Find the actual call before expecting the body to run.
call-01.mistake: Do not count a function body just because it appears above the output line.

print-not-return-01.title: Printing is not returning
print-not-return-01.body: Printing shows a value to the person. Returning hands a value back to the program.
print-not-return-01.notice: Check whether the function has a return value or only output side effects.
print-not-return-01.mistake: Do not store the result of a no-return function and expect a useful value instead of None.

return-value-01.title: Returned values replace the call
return-value-01.body: A function call with a return value can be used inside a larger expression.
return-value-01.notice: Evaluate each call, replace it with its returned value, then finish the expression.
return-value-01.mistake: Do not ignore the returned value when the next line uses it.

return-stops-01.title: Return exits immediately
return-stops-01.body: Once a return statement runs, the rest of that function call is over.
return-stops-01.notice: After an early return, skip later lines in the same function call.
return-stops-01.mistake: Do not keep executing a function after it has already returned.

missing-return-01.title: Every path needs a return plan
missing-return-01.body: If one branch returns but another branch reaches the end, the function may hand back no useful value.
missing-return-01.notice: Trace the path for the specific input, not only the branch that looks intended.
missing-return-01.mistake: Do not assume a skipped branch magically returns the other argument.

arg-order-01.title: Arguments fill parameters by position
arg-order-01.body: The first argument goes into the first parameter, the second into the second, and so on unless named arguments are used.
arg-order-01.notice: Write the parameter values before evaluating the body.
arg-order-01.mistake: Do not swap argument meaning because the names would sound nicer the other way.

local-scope-01.title: Local variables stay inside
local-scope-01.body: A value created inside a function or method is not automatically available outside it.
local-scope-01.notice: Use return values to move information out of a function.
local-scope-01.mistake: Do not print an inside-only name after the function has finished.

reuse-01.title: Each call runs fresh
reuse-01.body: Calling the same function more than once applies the same rule to new arguments.
reuse-01.notice: Evaluate each call separately, then combine the returned values.
reuse-01.mistake: Do not reuse the previous call's local parameter values.

function-in-condition-01.title: Boolean functions can drive decisions
function-in-condition-01.body: A function that returns true or false can be used directly as a condition.
function-in-condition-01.notice: Evaluate the returned boolean before choosing the branch.
function-in-condition-01.mistake: Do not print the boolean if the code uses it to choose an if or else path.

param-copy-01.title: Changing a parameter may not change the caller
param-copy-01.body: A parameter is the function's local name for the value it received.
param-copy-01.notice: If the function returns an updated value, the caller must store that return to keep it.
param-copy-01.mistake: Do not assume a local parameter assignment rewrites the original variable.
